subject: chemistry

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is burned in air and a white powder is left behind. Which statement about the magnesium is correct?
items.correct: The magnesium gains oxygen, so the magnesium is oxidised.
items.misconception: The magnesium gains oxygen, so it has been reduced.
items.why: The two labels are learnt as a pair and easily attach to the wrong half; 'reduce' feels like it should describe the change happening to the named substance. Fix the definitions to the oxygen, not to the substance: gain of oxygen is oxidation, loss of oxygen is reduction. Iron gains oxygen, so iron is oxidised.
items.random_wrong: The magnesium and the oxygen are simply mixed.

items.q: Copper is heated in air and a black solid forms on the surface. What is the black solid and what has happened to the copper?
items.correct: Copper oxide; the copper has been oxidised.
items.misconception: Copper oxide, though this is not an oxidation.
items.why: Oxidation is first met through dramatic burning demonstrations, so students tie the word to visible flames rather than to the gain of oxygen. Oxidation is defined by the gain of oxygen, however quiet the reaction looks. Copper heated in air gains oxygen to form copper oxide, so it is oxidised.
items.random_wrong: A mixture of copper and air joined on.

items.q: In the reaction 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, which substance is reduced, and why?
items.correct: Copper oxide, because it loses oxygen.
items.misconception: Carbon, because it gains oxygen in this.
items.why: Students remember that the two terms are opposites but not which way round, and 'reduction' has no obvious link to oxygen in ordinary language. Reduction is the loss of oxygen; oxidation is the gain of oxygen. In metal extraction the ore is reduced because oxygen is taken away from it.
items.random_wrong: Copper oxide, because the mass falls.

items.q: Which statement about oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen is correct?
items.correct: Oxidation is gain of oxygen; reduction is loss.
items.misconception: Reduction is gain of oxygen; oxidation is loss of it.
items.why: Students remember that the two terms are opposites but not which way round, and 'reduction' has no obvious link to oxygen in ordinary language. Reduction is the loss of oxygen; oxidation is the gain of oxygen. In metal extraction the ore is reduced because oxygen is taken away from it.
items.random_wrong: Reduction means the mass of the solid gets smaller.

items.q: A metal reacts with another substance. What happens to the metal atoms during the reaction?
items.correct: The metal atoms lose electrons and form positive ions.
items.misconception: The metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.
items.why: Reactions are seen as metals 'attacking' other substances, and taking rather than giving feels like the aggressive option. Metal atoms have few outer electrons and lose them. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a positive charge.
items.random_wrong: The metal atoms gain protons and become positive.

items.q: The reactivity of a metal is related to which property of its atoms?
items.correct: Its tendency to form positive ions.
items.misconception: Its tendency to grip its own electrons.
items.why: 'Reactive' is heard as 'strong', and holding on tightly sounds strong, so the reasoning runs the wrong way round. Reactivity of a metal is its tendency to form positive ions. The more easily a metal gives up its outer electrons, the more reactive it is.
items.random_wrong: How dense and hard the metal is.

items.q: From their reactions with water and with dilute acids, which metal is placed highest in the reactivity series?
items.correct: Potassium, as it reacts fast with cold water.
items.misconception: Copper, as it will not react with dilute acid.
items.why: The reactivity series is remembered as a list without a direction, so students read it upside down and let the weaker metal do the displacing. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Zinc is above copper, so zinc takes its place and copper metal is deposited.
items.random_wrong: Calcium, since it loses two electrons per atom.

items.q: The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series. Why?
items.correct: They are reference points to compare metals with.
items.misconception: They are included because they are unusual metals.
items.why: Everything else in the list is a metal, so students assume membership of the list implies being a metal. Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals. They are included so that metals can be compared with them, which is what decides how a metal is extracted.
items.random_wrong: They are placed there because every ore holds carbon.

items.q: A strip of magnesium is left in copper(II) sulfate solution. A pink-brown solid forms on the strip and the blue colour fades. Why?
items.correct: Magnesium is more reactive, so it displaces the copper.
items.misconception: Copper is more reactive, so it displaces magnesium.
items.why: The reactivity series is remembered as a list without a direction, so students read it upside down and let the weaker metal do the displacing. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Zinc is above copper, so zinc takes its place and copper metal is deposited.
items.random_wrong: Both are metals, so they simply swap places.

items.q: Which mixture will produce a displacement reaction?
items.correct: Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
items.misconception: Copper added to zinc sulfate solution.
items.why: The reactivity series is remembered as a list without a direction, so students read it upside down and let the weaker metal do the displacing. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Zinc is above copper, so zinc takes its place and copper metal is deposited.
items.random_wrong: Iron added to magnesium sulfate solution.

items.q: Which metal reacts with cold water at room temperature to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen?
items.correct: Sodium, which fizzes on the water surface.
items.misconception: Zinc, which bubbles steadily in cold water.
items.why: The dramatic demonstrations use potassium, sodium and lithium, and students generalise from the metals they have actually seen react. Only the metals from magnesium upwards react with cold water, and magnesium only very slowly. Zinc, iron and copper show no reaction with water at room temperature.
items.random_wrong: Copper, used in pipes that carry water.

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. What are the products?
items.correct: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
items.misconception: Magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas.
items.why: Metal oxides dominate the earlier work on oxidation, so the oxide is the product students expect from any metal reaction. A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen. With hydrochloric acid the salt is the chloride, so magnesium chloride forms.
items.random_wrong: Magnesium chloride and water only.

items.q: A piece of copper is left in dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Which statement describes what happens?
items.correct: Nothing happens, because copper is below hydrogen.
items.misconception: It fizzes steadily and gives off hydrogen.
items.why: Magnesium, zinc and iron all fizz, so the rule 'metal plus acid gives hydrogen' is taken to have no exceptions. A metal only displaces hydrogen from an acid if it is above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Copper is below hydrogen and does not react.
items.random_wrong: It reacts, but too slowly for bubbles to show.

items.q: Potassium reacts far more vigorously with cold water than magnesium does. What best explains this difference?
items.correct: Potassium loses its outer electron more readily.
items.misconception: Potassium holds on to its electrons more strongly.
items.why: 'Reactive' is heard as 'strong', and holding on tightly sounds strong, so the reasoning runs the wrong way round. Reactivity of a metal is its tendency to form positive ions. The more easily a metal gives up its outer electrons, the more reactive it is.
items.random_wrong: Potassium loses two electrons, magnesium one.

items.q: Metals X and Y are added to dilute acid. X fizzes vigorously while Y fizzes only slowly. What does this show about the atoms?
items.correct: X forms positive ions more readily than Y.
items.misconception: Y gives up its outer electrons more easily than X.
items.why: 'Reactive' is heard as 'strong', and holding on tightly sounds strong, so the reasoning runs the wrong way round. Reactivity of a metal is its tendency to form positive ions. The more easily a metal gives up its outer electrons, the more reactive it is.
items.random_wrong: X can form negative ions more readily than Y.

items.q: Four metals are added to dilute acid. P bubbles very fast, S bubbles moderately, Q bubbles slowly and R shows no change. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
items.correct: P, S, Q, R - fastest bubbling is most reactive.
items.misconception: R, Q, S, P - slowest bubbling means most reactive.
items.why: The reactivity series is remembered as a list without a direction, so students read it upside down and let the weaker metal do the displacing. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Zinc is above copper, so zinc takes its place and copper metal is deposited.
items.random_wrong: R, P, S, Q - no reaction at all means most reactive.

items.q: In separate tests, metal A displaces metal B from its sulfate solution, and metal B displaces metal C from its sulfate solution. What can be concluded?
items.correct: A is the most reactive of the three and C the least.
items.misconception: C is the most reactive and A the least reactive.
items.why: The reactivity series is remembered as a list without a direction, so students read it upside down and let the weaker metal do the displacing. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Zinc is above copper, so zinc takes its place and copper metal is deposited.
items.random_wrong: A and B are ordered, but C cannot be placed.

items.q: Gold is found in the Earth as the metal itself rather than as a compound. Why?
items.correct: Gold is unreactive, so it does not form compounds.
items.misconception: Gold was reduced by carbon deep underground long ago.
items.why: Carbon reduction is the extraction story students know, so it gets used to explain native metals as well. Native metals such as gold were never oxidised in the first place. No reduction is needed because no compound formed.
items.random_wrong: Gold is very rare, so too little of it can react.

items.q: Iron oxide is heated with carbon and iron metal is obtained. Why does this method work for iron?
items.correct: Iron is less reactive than carbon.
items.misconception: Iron is more reactive than the carbon.
items.why: The series is remembered as a list without a direction, so the carbon comparison is read the wrong way round; the metal being produced also feels like it ought to be the stronger one. Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal below it in the series. A successful carbon reduction shows the metal is less reactive than carbon, not more.
items.random_wrong: Carbon reduces every metal oxide.

items.q: Which metal cannot be extracted from its oxide by reduction with carbon?
items.correct: Potassium, which is above carbon.
items.misconception: Copper, which is well below carbon.
items.why: The series is remembered as a list without a direction, so the carbon comparison is read the wrong way round; the metal being produced also feels like it ought to be the stronger one. Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal below it in the series. A successful carbon reduction shows the metal is less reactive than carbon, not more.
items.random_wrong: Zinc, since carbon cannot reduce it.

items.q: What does the term reduction mean when a metal is obtained from its oxide?
items.correct: The oxide loses its oxygen and metal is left behind.
items.misconception: The oxide gains extra oxygen from the carbon.
items.why: Students remember that the two terms are opposites but not which way round, and 'reduction' has no obvious link to oxygen in ordinary language. Reduction is the loss of oxygen; oxidation is the gain of oxygen. In metal extraction the ore is reduced because oxygen is taken away from it.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the solid in the furnace falls.

items.q: A furnace is charged with lead(II) oxide and carbon. The reaction is 2PbO + C -> 2Pb + CO2. Which statement about this process is correct?
items.correct: Lead is below carbon in the reactivity series.
items.misconception: Lead lies above carbon in the reactivity series.
items.why: The series is remembered as a list without a direction, so the carbon comparison is read the wrong way round; the metal being produced also feels like it ought to be the stronger one. Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal below it in the series. A successful carbon reduction shows the metal is less reactive than carbon, not more.
items.random_wrong: Carbon is reduced and lead oxide is oxidised.

items.q: A student is told that a metal M is found in the Earth as its oxide and that M is obtained by heating that oxide with carbon. What can be deduced about M?
items.correct: M is less reactive than carbon is.
items.misconception: M must be more reactive than carbon.
items.why: The series is remembered as a list without a direction, so the carbon comparison is read the wrong way round; the metal being produced also feels like it ought to be the stronger one. Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal below it in the series. A successful carbon reduction shows the metal is less reactive than carbon, not more.
items.random_wrong: M is just as unreactive as gold.

items.q: In the reaction 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2, which substance is oxidised?
items.correct: Carbon, because it gains oxygen.
items.misconception: Carbon, because it loses oxygen here.
items.why: Carbon is described as the reducing agent, and the word 'reducing' next to 'carbon' is read as a label for what happens to the carbon. Apply the definition to the oxygen. Carbon gains oxygen, so carbon is oxidised even though it is the substance that reduces the copper oxide.
items.random_wrong: Iron oxide, because it gains oxygen.

items.q: In terms of electrons, which statement is correct?
items.correct: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain.
items.misconception: Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction the loss.
items.why: Oxidation is first learnt as gain of oxygen, so 'gain' becomes attached to the word and is carried over to electrons. Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain - of electrons. A substance that loses electrons is oxidised; one that gains electrons is reduced.
items.random_wrong: Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction the gain.

items.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, which species is oxidised and why?
items.correct: Zinc, because it loses its two electrons.
items.misconception: Zinc, since it gains two electrons.
items.why: Oxidation is first learnt as gain of oxygen, so 'gain' becomes attached to the word and is carried over to electrons. Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain - of electrons. A substance that loses electrons is oxidised; one that gains electrons is reduced.
items.random_wrong: The copper ion, because it loses electrons.

items.q: Magnesium is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which is the correct ionic equation?
items.correct: Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
items.misconception: Mg + CuSO4 -> MgSO4 + Cu
items.why: The full symbol equation is written first and the sulfate is copied straight across without asking whether it changed. Sulfate ions are unchanged spectators, so they are left out. The ionic equation shows only Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu.
items.random_wrong: 2Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu

items.q: Which half equation shows a species being reduced?
items.correct: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, a gain of electrons.
items.misconception: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, a gain of two electrons.
items.why: Oxidation is first learnt as gain of oxygen, so 'gain' becomes attached to the word and is carried over to electrons. Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain - of electrons. A substance that loses electrons is oxidised; one that gains electrons is reduced.
items.random_wrong: Mg + 2e- -> Mg2+, electrons are taken in.

items.q: In 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, what does it mean to say the copper oxide is reduced?
items.correct: The copper oxide loses its oxygen to the carbon.
items.misconception: Reduced means there is less of it, so the solid has simply got smaller or lighter.
items.why: In everyday English 'reduce' means to make smaller, and the solid in the crucible really does lose mass, which seems to confirm the guess. In chemistry reduction has a fixed meaning: loss of oxygen. The mass falls because oxygen has been removed, but the falling mass is a consequence, not the definition.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Magnesium burns in air to leave a white powder. What is the white powder?
items.correct: Magnesium oxide, a new compound of magnesium and oxygen.
items.misconception: It is just magnesium with oxygen mixed into it, so no new substance has been made.
items.why: The powder still comes from the same lump of metal, and students who have just studied mixtures reach for the idea that is freshest. The metal and oxygen are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and the product has completely different properties. A metal oxide is a compound, not a mixture.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, is anything oxidised as well as reduced?
items.correct: Yes - the copper oxide is reduced and the carbon is oxidised in the same reaction.
items.misconception: A reaction is either an oxidation or a reduction, so only one of the two can be happening.
items.why: The two words are taught in separate lessons and as separate definitions, so students file them as alternatives rather than as two halves of one change. Oxygen removed from one substance has to go somewhere. Whenever something loses oxygen, something else gains it, so reduction and oxidation occur together.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can you predict a metal's reactivity from how dense or how hard it is?
items.correct: No - reactivity depends on the tendency of the metal to form positive ions.
items.misconception: Reactivity follows the physical properties: a hard, dense metal is a strong, reactive metal.
items.why: Physical properties are the ones students can see and handle, so they are borrowed to explain a chemical property that has no visible cause. Sodium is soft and light yet extremely reactive; iron is hard and dense yet far less reactive. Reactivity is about electron loss, not hardness or density.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A magnesium atom reacts with dilute acid. What happens to the atom?
items.correct: It loses two electrons and becomes a magnesium ion.
items.misconception: It stays as a neutral atom and simply joins on to the other substance.
items.why: Students picture reaction as sticking particles together, so nothing needs to change inside the atom. When metals react the metal atoms form positive ions. Electrons are transferred away from the metal, so the atom does not survive unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a metal atom become positively charged?
items.correct: By losing negatively charged electrons.
items.misconception: By gaining protons, since protons are the positive particles.
items.why: Charge is correctly linked to protons, and the quickest way to add positive charge seems to be to add protons. Protons are locked in the nucleus and never move in chemical reactions. Removing electrons leaves the proton count unchanged but the overall charge positive.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Will copper displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate solution?
items.correct: No - copper is less reactive than magnesium, so no reaction occurs.
items.misconception: Yes - any metal can displace any other metal from its solution.
items.why: Displacement is remembered as something metals do, without the condition that decides whether it happens at all. Displacement only happens one way. The metal added must be above the metal in the compound in the reactivity series, otherwise there is no reaction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Calcium loses two electrons and potassium loses one. Which is more reactive?
items.correct: Potassium is more reactive, even though it loses only one electron.
items.misconception: Calcium must be more reactive because it loses twice as many electrons.
items.why: More electrons lost looks like more chemistry happening, so quantity is mistaken for ease. Reactivity depends on how readily electrons are lost, not how many. Potassium's single outer electron is lost far more easily than calcium's two.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a heavier metal atom mean a more reactive metal?
items.correct: No - relative atomic mass does not set the order of reactivity.
items.misconception: Reactivity increases with relative atomic mass, so copper and iron beat sodium.
items.why: Within a single group reactivity does increase down the group, and students over-extend that pattern across the whole series. The reactivity series runs potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper - light sodium is far above heavy copper.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is carbon placed in the reactivity series?
items.correct: So that metals can be compared with carbon, which decides if carbon can extract them.
items.misconception: Because every ore contains carbon, so carbon has to be in the list.
items.why: Coke appears in the blast furnace and carbonate ores contain carbon, so carbon seems to be part of the ore itself. Carbon is placed in the series purely for comparison. Metals below carbon can be reduced by it; metals above it cannot, whatever the ore contains.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can carbon be used to extract every metal from its oxide?
items.correct: No - only metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted this way.
items.misconception: Yes - carbon will reduce any metal oxide if it is heated hot enough.
items.why: Carbon reduction is the only extraction method studied in detail, so it is taken to be universal. Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal that holds it less strongly than carbon does. Metals above carbon, such as potassium, need a different method.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Potassium is above carbon in the reactivity series. Can carbon reduce potassium oxide?
items.correct: No - potassium holds its oxygen too strongly for carbon to remove it.
items.misconception: Yes - being above carbon just means the reaction needs more heat.
items.why: Students treat position in the series as a measure of difficulty rather than of whether the reaction can happen. Position in the series decides whether carbon reduction works at all. A metal above carbon cannot be extracted from its oxide by carbon, at any temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is iron oxide heated with carbon rather than heated on its own?
items.correct: Because carbon is needed to remove the oxygen from the iron oxide.
items.misconception: Because the heat just melts the ore and lets the iron run out of it.
items.why: The furnace is obviously hot and molten metal pours out, so the change looks like melting rather than a chemical reaction. Iron in an ore is chemically combined with oxygen. Melting cannot separate them; a reduction reaction with carbon is needed to take the oxygen away.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is gold found in the Earth as the metal itself?
items.correct: Because gold is so unreactive that it does not readily form compounds.
items.misconception: Because gold is rare, so there is too little of it to react with anything.
items.why: Rarity and being found as the metal are two facts learnt about gold together, so one is used to explain the other. How much of a metal there is has no bearing on whether it reacts. Gold is found native because it is very unreactive, not because it is scarce.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is gold not found combined as an oxide?
items.correct: Because gold is too unreactive to combine with oxygen.
items.misconception: Because gold is so dense that it sinks below the ores and stays pure.
items.why: Panning for gold works by density, so density becomes the explanation for everything about gold. Density explains how gold is separated from sand, not why it is uncombined. Being unreactive is what keeps gold as the free metal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper is used for water pipes. What does this tell you about copper and water?
items.correct: That copper does not react with water at room temperature.
items.misconception: That copper must react with water, since it is always in contact with it.
items.why: Being used with water is read as evidence of a relationship with water, rather than of the absence of one. Copper is chosen for pipes precisely because it does not react with the water it carries. Contact is not reaction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Iron rusts in damp air. Does iron react with cold water in the laboratory?
items.correct: No - iron shows no reaction when placed in cold water at room temperature.
items.misconception: Yes - rusting proves that iron reacts with cold water quite quickly.
items.why: Rusting is the one iron-and-water change students know, and it is assumed to be the same reaction as the ones being compared here. Rusting needs both water and oxygen and takes days or weeks. In the reactivity test with cold water, iron gives no hydrogen and no reaction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does magnesium plus dilute hydrochloric acid produce water?
items.correct: No - the products are magnesium chloride and hydrogen only.
items.misconception: Yes - acid reactions always give a salt plus water.
items.why: The neutralisation pattern acid + base -> salt + water is learnt thoroughly and then applied to a metal, which is not a base. Acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen. Only acid with a metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate produces water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which gas is given off when zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.correct: Hydrogen.
items.misconception: Chlorine, because chlorine is part of hydrochloric acid.
items.why: The name of the acid contains 'chloric', so the gas released is assumed to be the chlorine that is named. The chloride stays behind in the salt, zinc chloride. The gas released is hydrogen, which pops with a lighted splint.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper is left in dilute hydrochloric acid. Does the acid turn blue?
items.correct: No - copper does not react with dilute acid, so the acid stays colourless.
items.misconception: The acid turns blue because the copper dissolves to give a copper salt.
items.why: Copper compounds met in class are blue, so any container holding copper is expected to turn blue. A blue solution would need a copper compound to form, and no reaction occurs at all. Copper is below hydrogen and dilute acid leaves it unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper in dilute acid shows nothing at all. What does that mean?
items.correct: There is no reaction between copper and dilute acid.
items.misconception: There is a reaction, but it is far too slow to see any bubbles.
items.why: 'No reaction' feels like an unsatisfying answer, so students assume something must be happening below the limit of sight. Copper does not react with dilute acid at all. No reaction is a valid and important experimental result, and it places copper below hydrogen.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two metals are compared. Does the one with more electrons react faster?
items.correct: No - what matters is how readily the outer electrons are lost.
items.misconception: The metal whose atoms contain more electrons in total is more reactive.
items.why: Reactivity is linked to electrons, so students reach for the electron number they can count from the atomic number. Only the outer electrons are transferred. Copper atoms have far more electrons than sodium atoms yet copper is much less reactive.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A metal shows no bubbles at all in dilute acid. Where does it go in the series?
items.correct: At the bottom - no reaction means it is the least reactive metal tested.
items.misconception: At the top, because a metal strong enough to resist the acid must be the most reactive.
items.why: 'Unreactive' is heard as weak and 'resists attack' is heard as strong, and the two readings pull in opposite directions. Reactivity is measured by how readily the metal reacts. A metal that does not react at all with dilute acid is the least reactive of the set.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A metal gives no reaction with water or with dilute acid. Can it be placed in the series?
items.correct: Yes - the absence of a reaction places it below the metals that did react.
items.misconception: No - a metal that does not react gives no information, so it cannot be ranked.
items.why: Students treat a negative result as a failed experiment rather than as evidence. A negative result is evidence. Showing no reaction where others do react places the metal at the bottom of the order.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A displaces B, and B displaces C. What can you say about A and C?
items.correct: A is more reactive than C, so A would displace C as well.
items.misconception: Nothing - A and C were never tested together, so they cannot be compared.
items.why: Students stick strictly to what was observed and do not see that the two results chain together into one order. The results give a single order: A above B above C. That order lets you predict the untested pair, and the prediction can then be checked.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. What has the zinc lost?
items.correct: Two electrons.
items.misconception: Two protons, which is why the charge on the ion is 2+.
items.why: The 2+ charge is correctly linked to positive particles, and protons are the positive particles students name first. The half equation shows 2e- released, so the zinc has lost two electrons. Proton number never changes in a chemical reaction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, are both species losing electrons?
items.correct: No - zinc loses electrons and the copper ion gains them.
items.misconception: Both species lose electrons, because both are changing during the reaction.
items.why: Electron loss is the half of the definition students recall first, and it gets applied to everything that changes. Electrons transferred from one species must be gained by another. Oxidation and reduction are two halves of the same electron transfer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, is the copper ion oxidised or reduced?
items.correct: It is reduced, because it gains two electrons to become copper metal.
items.misconception: It is oxidised, because it turns into a metal you can see forming.
items.why: A visible product looks like the main event, and students label the change they can see as the oxidation. Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu shows electrons being gained, and gain of electrons is reduction. The copper ion is reduced.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg+ + Cu a correct ionic equation?
items.correct: No - magnesium forms Mg2+, and the charges must balance.
items.misconception: Yes - it shows magnesium becoming an ion and copper becoming a metal.
items.why: Attention goes to which substances appear rather than to the charges, so an unbalanced charge slips through unnoticed. Charge must balance across an ionic or half equation. Magnesium loses both outer electrons, so the correct equation is Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is 2Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu a correct ionic equation?
items.correct: No - putting a 2 in front of Mg unbalances the magnesium atoms.
items.misconception: A number can be put in front of a formula to make the charges match up.
items.why: Balancing symbol equations is done by adjusting big numbers, so the same move is tried when the charges do not look right. Big numbers balance atoms, not charges. Charge is balanced by using the correct ion, Mg2+, so the equation is Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu.

items.q: The blue colour of copper(II) sulfate solution fades when magnesium is added. Why?
items.correct: Because copper ions are being removed from the solution as copper metal.
items.misconception: Because the solution has been watered down or the colour has spread out.
items.why: Fading is associated in everyday life with dilution or with a stain spreading, so a physical explanation is reached for first. Nothing has been added to dilute the solution. The blue colour fades because the blue copper ions are used up and replaced by colourless magnesium ions.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu, should both metals be written as ions?
items.correct: No - only one is an ion on each side of the equation.
items.misconception: Both should be shown as ions, since ionic equations are about ions.
items.why: The name 'ionic equation' suggests everything in it must be written as an ion. An ionic equation shows ions only where they actually exist. Magnesium starts as a metal atom and copper finishes as a metal atom.
